---
title: "Applications"
lang: en
---

In this chapter we introduce the composition of two forcing notions.
We show that every partial order is completely embedded into the
composition of itself with any other forcing notion. We study examples
of interest for the composition of a partial order with itself, and
analyse the interaction of this composition with its quotient modulo a
generic filter (see @def-moduloG). Finally, we define a separative
partial order and give two different ways of densely embedding every
partial order into two separative notions, not necessarily isomorphic
to each other.

## Composition

In this section we set out to answer a question that, as Saharon
Shelah does in [@shelah], can be phrased as follows: suppose we start
with a model $V$ and, via a forcing notion $\mathbb P$, extend it to
$V[G]$, where $G$ is a generic subset of $\mathbb P$; we then take a
forcing notion $\mathbb Q$ in $V[G]$ and extend $V[G]$ to $V[G][H]$,
where $H$ is a generic filter on $\mathbb Q$. Is it possible to obtain
the extension $V[G][H]$ from $V$ by a single forcing extension? The
concepts and results below will give a positive answer to our
question.

::: {#def-pnombre-orden}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ be a partial order.

We say that the triple of $\mathbb P$-names
$(\dot{\mathbb Q}, \dot{\leq}, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in V$ is
a **$\mathbb P$-name for a partial order** if
$\mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}} \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$
and
$$
\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P} \Vdash
[(\mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}} \in \dot{\mathbb Q}) \,\&\,
 (\dot{\leq} \text{ is a partial order on } \dot{\mathbb Q}
  \text{ whose maximum element is } \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})].
$$
:::

For simplicity, we will simply write $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ to refer to the
$\mathbb P$-name given by the triple
$(\dot{\mathbb Q}, \dot{\leq}, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$ of the
previous definition. In this context, by $\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$ we
mean $\{\dot{\mathbb Q}, \dot{\leq}, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}\}
\subseteq V$. Also, $\mathbb{1}$ will denote the maximum element
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$.

::: {#def-composicion}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order in $V$ and $\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$
the $\mathbb P$-name of a partial order. We define **$\mathbb P$
composed with $\dot{\mathbb Q}$** as
$$
\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q} = \{(p, \dot x) :
p \in \mathbb P \,\&\, \dot x \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}
\,\&\, p \Vdash \dot x \in \dot{\mathbb Q}\}.
$$

Also, given $(p, \dot x), (q, \dot y) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$
we define
$$
(p, \dot x) \leq (q, \dot y) \quad\text{iff}\quad
p \leq_{\mathbb P} q \;\text{and}\; p \Vdash \dot x\,\dot{\leq}\,\dot y.
$$

Finally, $\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}} =
(\mathbb{1}, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.
:::

Note that $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$, since both $\mathbb P$
and $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ are elements of $V$ and, by
@thm-teoremadeforcing (1), the notion $\Vdash$ is equivalent to one
that can be relativised to $V$.

**Remark.** For every $p \in \mathbb P$,
$(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$.
This holds since by @def-pnombre-orden,
$\mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}} \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$
and $\mathbb{1} \Vdash \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}} \in
\dot{\mathbb Q}$. Since $p \leq \mathbb{1}$, by
@lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$p \Vdash \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}} \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$, which
verifies the observation.

We now show that if the valuation of a $\mathbb P$-name with respect
to a generic filter $G$ is an element of the notion $\mathbb Q$, where
$\mathbb Q = \dot{\mathbb Q}_G \in V[G]$, then there is a pair in the
composition $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ whose second coordinate is
forced by the first to equal the $\mathbb P$-name we started with.

::: {#lem-caballito}
Let $\mathbb P$ and $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ be as in the previous
definition. If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter,
$\mathbb Q = \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$ and $\dot q \in V^{\mathbb P}$
satisfies $\dot q_G \in \mathbb Q$, then there is
$(p, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ such that $p \in G$
and $p \Vdash \dot q = \dot q_0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @thm-teoremadeforcing (2), for some $r \in G$,
$r \Vdash \exists x \, (x \in \dot{\mathbb Q} \,\&\, x = \dot q)$. By
@lem-nombreeneldominio, there are $p \in G$ and
$\dot q_0 \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$ with $p \leq r$ and
$p \Vdash \dot q_0 = \dot q$. So by @def-composicion,
$(p, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$.
:::

Whenever context is clear, we will simplify the notation in the
following results by writing $\leq$ instead of $\dot{\leq}$.

::: {#prp-composicion-es-orden}
If $\mathbb P$ is a partial order and $\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$ is the
$\mathbb P$-name of a partial order, then $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$
is a partial order.
:::

::: {.proof}
$(p, \dot x) \leq (p, \dot x)$ because $p \leq p$ and
$p \Vdash \dot x \leq \dot x$. If $(p, \dot x) \leq (q, \dot y)$ and
$(q, \dot y) \leq (r, \dot z)$, then $p \leq q$,
$p \Vdash \dot x \leq \dot y$, $q \leq r$ and
$q \Vdash \dot y \leq \dot z$. So $p \leq r$ and
$p \Vdash \dot y \leq \dot z$. Hence
$p \Vdash \dot x \leq \dot z$.
:::

::: {#def-inclusioncomposicion}
Let $i : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ be the function
defined by $i(p) = (p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.
:::

Note that $i \in V$. This follows because
$\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$. For the rest of the section, $i$
will always denote the function of the previous definition. In this
vein, the next lemma concludes that via the function $i$, every
partial order is completely embedded into the composition we have
been talking about.

::: {#lem-encajeiteracion}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ be a partial order and $\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$
the $\mathbb P$-name for a partial order. Then:

1. For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \leq q$ if and only if
   $(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \leq (q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.
2. $i(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}) = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}}$.
3. If $(p, \dot x), (q, \dot y) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ and
   $p \perp q$, then $(p, \dot x) \perp (q, \dot y)$.
4. For every $(p, \dot x) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ and
   $q \in \mathbb P$, $p \perp q$ if and only if
   $(p, \dot x) \perp (q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.
5. For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \perp q$ if and only if
   $i(p) \perp i(q)$.
6. The function $i : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ is a
   complete embedding.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1). Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$. If $p \leq q$, since
$p \Vdash \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}} \leq \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}$,
$(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \leq (q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.
Conversely, if
$(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \leq (q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$,
by @def-composicion $p \leq q$.

(2). By @def-inclusioncomposicion and @def-composicion,
$i(\mathbb{1}) = (\mathbb{1}, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) =
\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}}$.

(3). By contrapositive. Suppose $(p, \dot x) \mid (q, \dot y)$. Then
$(r, \dot z) \leq (p, \dot x), (q, \dot y)$ for some
$(r, \dot z) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. Hence $p \mid q$.

(4). Since
$(q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
the left-to-right implication follows from (3). We prove the
converse by contrapositive. If $r \leq p, q$ for some
$r \in \mathbb P$, by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1)
$r \Vdash \dot x \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$, hence
$(r, \dot x) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. Also
$r \Vdash \dot x \leq \dot x$ and
$r \Vdash \dot x \leq \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}$. So
$(r, \dot x) \leq (p, \dot x), (q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.

(5). Follows from (4) applied to the pairs
$(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}), (q, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})
\in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$.

(6). By (1) and (5), $i$ preserves order and incompatibility. So
$i : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ is an embedding.

We prove $i$ is a complete embedding using the equivalence of
@thm-equivalenciaencaje. Let
$(p, \dot x) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ be arbitrary. Take any
$q \leq p$. In particular, $q \mid p$. Hence, by (4),
$(p, \dot x) \mid i(q)$, that is, $p$ is an $i$-reduction of
$(p, \dot x)$ to $\mathbb P$.
:::

We now analyse the connections between the generic filters of
$\mathbb P$ and $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ with respect to those of
$\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$.

::: {#def-iteracionfiltros}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order and $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ the
$\mathbb P$-name of a partial order. If $G$ is a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter and $H \subseteq \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$,
we define
$$
G * H = \{(p, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q} :
         p \in G \,\&\, \dot q_G \in H\}.
$$
:::

A first sample from our analysis is that the generic filters of
$\mathbb P$ and $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ are determined by their composition,
as the next result shows.

::: {#lem-igualdadgenericos}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ be a partial order, and $\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$
the $\mathbb P$-name of a partial order. Let $G$ be a
$(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter and let $\mathbb Q = \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$.
If $H$ is a $(V[G], \mathbb Q)$-generic filter, then:

1. $G = \{p : \exists \dot q \, ((p, \dot q) \in G * H)\}$.
2. $H = \{\dot q_G : \exists p \, ((p, \dot q) \in G * H)\}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1). If $p \in G$, then
$i(p) = (p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in G * H$, since
$(\mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})_G \in H$. This same argument shows
$p \in i^{-1}[G * H]$, that is, $G \subseteq i^{-1}[G * H]$. The
remaining containment holds: given $p \in \mathbb P$ such that
$(p, \dot q) \in G * H$ for some $\dot q \in V^{\mathbb P}$, by
@def-iteracionfiltros $p \in G$.

(2). If $q \in H \subseteq \mathbb Q$, then $q = \dot q_G$ for some
$\dot q \in V^{\mathbb P}$. So by @lem-caballito, there is
$(p_0, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ with $p_0 \in G$ and
$p_0 \Vdash \dot q_0 = \dot q$. But then $(\dot q_0)_G = q \in H$, so
by @def-iteracionfiltros, $(p_0, \dot q_0) \in G * H$, which proves
the first containment. Conversely, if
$x \in \{\dot q_G : \exists p \, ((p, \dot q) \in G * H)\}$, there
is $(p, \dot q) \in G * H$ with $\dot q_G = x$, and since
$\dot q_G \in H$, the result holds.
:::

The next theorem presents the following situation: in $V[G]$, the
generic extension given by $\mathbb P$, $\dot{\mathbb Q}_G = \mathbb Q$
is a partial order, so it makes sense to force with $\mathbb Q$ over
$V[G]$. Denote by $V[G][H]$ this latter forcing extension, where $H$
is a generic filter on $\mathbb Q$. The theorem states that $V[G][H]$
coincides with the extension given by the composition
$\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. In this way we answer the question
posed at the start of the section: $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ is
the forcing notion in $V$ that we were looking for.

::: {#thm-iteraciondos}
Let $\mathbb P, \dot{\mathbb Q}, G$ and $H$ be as in the previous
lemma. Then:

1. $G * H$ is a $(V, \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})$-generic filter.
2. $V[G * H] = V[G][H]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove $G * H$ is a filter. Let
$(p_0, \dot q_0), (p_1, \dot q_1) \in G * H$. Then $p_0, p_1 \in G$
and $(\dot q_0)_G, (\dot q_1)_G \in H$. So there are $r \in G$ and
$x \in H$ with $r \leq p_0, p_1$ and
$x \leq (\dot q_0)_G, (\dot q_1)_G$. By @lem-igualdadgenericos (2),
there is $(p, \dot q) \in G * H$ with $x = \dot q_G$. By
@def-iteracionfiltros, $p \in G$. Now, by @thm-teoremadeforcing (2),
there is $t \in G$ with $t \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q_0, \dot q_1$. By
@prp-extensionparamuchos, there is $s \in G$ with
$s \leq r, p, t$. Observe that since
$(p, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$, by
@def-composicion, $\dot q \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$ and
$p \Vdash \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$. So by
@lem-alguienmasfuerte (1), $s \Vdash \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
which guarantees $(s, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. Now,
since $s \leq t$, by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1)
$s \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q_0, \dot q_1$. Since $\dot q_G \in H$,
$(s, \dot q) \in G * H$ and
$(s, \dot q) \leq (p_0, \dot q_0), (p_1, \dot q_1)$.

Suppose now that $(p_0, \dot q_0) \in G * H$ and
$(p, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ satisfy
$(p_0, \dot q_0) \leq (p, \dot q)$. Then by @def-composicion,
$p_0 \leq p$ and $p_0 \Vdash \dot q_0 \leq \dot q$. Since
$p_0 \in G$, $p \in G$ and $(\dot q_0)_G \leq (\dot q)_G$. By
hypothesis $(\dot q_0)_G \in H$, hence $\dot q_G \in H$. So
$(p, \dot q) \in G * H$.

We prove the genericity of $G * H$. Let $D \in V$ be any dense
subset of $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$.

We first verify that
$E = \{\dot q_G : \exists p \in G \, ((p, \dot q) \in D)\}$ is a
dense subset of $\mathbb Q$. Let $q \in \mathbb Q$ be arbitrary. So
$q = \dot s_G$ for some $\dot s \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$.
By @lem-caballito, there is
$(p_0, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ with $p_0 \in G$ and
$p_0 \Vdash \dot s = \dot q_0$. Define
$$
E_1 = \{p \in \mathbb P : \exists x \, (p \Vdash x \leq \dot q_0
                                        \,\&\, (p, x) \in D)\}.
$$

We claim $E_1$ is dense below $p_0$. Let $r \leq p_0$. By
@lem-alguienmasfuerte (1), $r \Vdash \dot q_0 \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$.
Hence $(r, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. Since $D$ is
dense in $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$, $(p, x) \leq (r, \dot q_0)$
for some $(p, x) \in D$. By @def-composicion,
$p \Vdash x \leq \dot q_0$. Hence $p \leq r$ and $p \in E_1$.

Now, $E_1 \in V$ because $\mathbb P, D, \dot q_0 \in V$
($\dot q_0 \in V$, since $\dot q_0 \in \operatorname{dom}
\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$ and $V$ is transitive). Since $p_0 \in G$, by
@lem-lemadenso (2) $G \cap E_1 \neq \emptyset$. Let
$p \in G \cap E_1$. Then $p \in G$ and for some $x$,
$p \Vdash x \leq \dot q_0$ and $(p, x) \in D$. Note that since
$D \subseteq \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$, $x = (\dot q_1)_G$ for
some $\dot q_1 \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$. So
$(\dot q_1)_G \leq (\dot q_0)_G = \dot s_G = q$. So
$(\dot q_1)_G \leq q$ and $(\dot q_1)_G \in E$, proving the density
of $E$.

$E \in V[G]$, since $G \in V[G]$ and $D \in V \subseteq V[G]$. By
the genericity of $H$, $H \cap E \neq \emptyset$. So there is
$(p, \dot q) \in D$ with $\dot q_G \in H$ and $p \in G$. Hence
$(p, \dot q) \in D \cap (G * H)$, proving the genericity of $G * H$.

Finally, we prove (2). On one hand,
$G \in V[G] \subseteq V[G][H]$ and $H \in V[G][H]$, so
$G * H \in V[G][H]$. By @lem-minimalidad,
$V[G * H] \subseteq V[G][H]$. On the other hand, we have proved that
$G * H$ is a $(V, \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})$-generic filter and
since the embedding $i : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$
is complete (see @lem-encajeiteracion), by @thm-encajeuno
$i^{-1}[G * H]$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter. Since
$G \subseteq i^{-1}[G * H]$ (see the proof of
@lem-igualdadgenericos (1)), @lem-filtrosiguales gives
$G = i^{-1}[G * H]$. So by @thm-encajeuno,
$V[G] \subseteq V[G * H]$, hence $G \in V[G * H]$ since $G \in V[G]$.
Also, by @lem-igualdadgenericos, $H = \{\dot q_G : \exists p \,
((p, \dot q) \in G * H)\}$, and since $G * H \in V[G * H]$,
$H \in V[G * H]$. So by @lem-minimalidad,
$V[G][H] \subseteq V[G * H]$. This proves the equality of the
extensions.
:::

Schematically: $\mathbb P \leq_c \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
$\dot{\mathbb Q}_G = \mathbb Q$ lets one force on $V[G]$, and the
composition $G * H$ is the $(V, \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})$-generic
filter that returns the two-step extension $V[G][H]$:
$$
V \;\subseteq\; V[G] \;\subseteq\; V[G][H] \;=\; V[G * H],
\qquad G * H \subseteq \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}.
$$

A converse of the previous theorem follows. This result will show
that every generic filter for $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ is of the
form $G * H$ for certain filters $G$ and $H$.

::: {#thm-iteracionuno}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ be a partial order and let
$\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$ be a $\mathbb P$-name for a partial order.
If $K$ is a $(V, \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})$-generic filter,
$H = \{\dot q_G : \exists r \, ((r, \dot q) \in K)\}$ and
$G = i^{-1}[K]$, then:

1. $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter.
2. $H$ is a $(V[G], \mathbb Q)$-generic filter, where
   $\mathbb Q = \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$.
3. $K = G * H$.
4. $V[K] = V[G][H]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-encajeiteracion (6), $i$ is a complete embedding. So by
@thm-encajeuno, $G = i^{-1}[K]$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter.

We verify $H$ is a filter. Let $p_0, p_1 \in H$. Then there are
$(r_0, \dot q_0), (r_1, \dot q_1) \in K$ with
$\dot q_0, \dot q_1 \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
$(\dot q_0)_G = p_0$ and $(\dot q_1)_G = p_1$.
@prp-extensionparamuchos guarantees there is $(r, \dot q) \in K$ with
$(r, \dot q) \leq (r_0, \dot q_0), (r_1, \dot q_1)$. So
$r \leq r_0, r_1$ and $r \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q_0$ and
$r \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q_1$. Also
$(r, \dot q) \leq (r, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$, so
$i(r) = (r, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in K$, hence $r \in G$.
Therefore $\dot q_G \in H$ and
$\dot q_G \leq (\dot q_0)_G, (\dot q_1)_G$.

Let $p \in H$ and $q \in \mathbb Q$ with $p \leq q$. So there are
$(r, \dot q_0) \in K$ and $\dot q \in V^{\mathbb P}$ with
$\dot q_0, \dot q \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
$(\dot q_0)_G = p$ and $\dot q_G = q$. By @thm-teoremadeforcing (2),
for some $p_0 \in G$, $p_0 \Vdash \dot q_0, \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$
and $p_0 \Vdash \dot q_0 \leq \dot q$. Observe that since
$p_0 \in G = i^{-1}[K]$,
$i(p_0) = (p_0, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in K$. Let
$(r_1, \dot q_1) \in K$ with
$(r_1, \dot q_1) \leq (r, \dot q_0), (p_0, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$.
By @def-composicion, $r_1 \Vdash \dot q_1 \leq \dot q_0$ and
$r_1 \leq p_0$. From this latter inequality and by
@lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$r_1 \Vdash \dot q_0 \leq \dot q$ and
$r_1 \Vdash \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$. Hence
$r_1 \Vdash \dot q_1 \leq \dot q$ and
$(r_1, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. But then
$(r_1, \dot q_1) \leq (r_1, \dot q)$, so $(r_1, \dot q) \in K$.
Hence $\dot q_G = q \in H$.

We prove the genericity of $H$. Let $D \in V[G]$ be a dense subset
of $\dot{\mathbb Q}_G$. So there is $\dot D \in V^{\mathbb P}$ with
$\dot D_G = D$. By @thm-teoremadeforcing (2), for some $p \in G$,
$p \Vdash \dot D$ is dense in $\dot{\mathbb Q}$. Define
$$
E = \{(r, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q} :
     r \Vdash \dot q \in \dot D\}.
$$

We claim $E$ is dense below $(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$. Let
$(p_0, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ with
$(p_0, \dot q_0) \leq (p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$. So
$p_0 \leq p$, hence by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1)
$p_0 \Vdash \dot D$ is dense in $\dot{\mathbb Q}$, and since also
$p_0 \Vdash \dot q_0 \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
$p_0 \Vdash \exists x \, (x \in \dot{\mathbb Q} \,\&\, x \in \dot D
\,\&\, x \leq \dot q_0)$. By @lem-nombreeneldominio (1), there are
$r \in \mathbb P$ and $\dot q_1 \in \operatorname{dom}
\dot{\mathbb Q}$ with $r \leq p_0$ and
$r \Vdash (\dot q_1 \in \dot D \,\&\, \dot q_1 \leq \dot q_0)$. So
by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (2),
$r \Vdash \dot q_1 \in \dot D \subseteq \dot{\mathbb Q}$ and
$r \Vdash \dot q_1 \leq \dot q_0$. So
$(r, \dot q_1) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ with
$(r, \dot q_1) \in E$ and $(r, \dot q_1) \leq (p_0, \dot q_0)$,
which proves the claim.

Since $\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q} \in V \subseteq V[G]$ and
$D \in V[G]$, $E \in V[G]$. Now,
$(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in K$ and $E$ is dense below
$(p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$, so by @lem-lemadenso (2),
$K \cap E \neq \emptyset$. Let $(r, \dot q) \in K \cap E$. Then
$(r, \dot q) \in K$ and since
$(r, \dot q) \leq (r, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$,
$(r, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) \in K$, which implies $r \in G$.
Also $\dot q_G \in H$, while $(r, \dot q) \in E$ implies
$r \Vdash \dot q \in \dot D$. So $\dot q_G \in D \cap H$.

We now prove (3). If $(p, \dot q) \in K$, then $p \in G$ since
$G = i^{-1}[K]$ (recall
$(p, \dot q) \leq (p, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}) = i(p)$, hence
$i(p) \in K$, so $p \in G$). Since
$K \subseteq \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$,
$\dot q \in \operatorname{dom} \dot{\mathbb Q}$. So by the
definition of $H$, $\dot q_G \in H$. Hence $K \subseteq G * H$. But
by @thm-iteraciondos $G * H$ is a $(V, \mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q})$-generic filter, so by @lem-filtrosiguales,
$K = G * H$.

Finally, (4) holds since by (3) $K = G * H$, so
@thm-iteraciondos (2) gives $V[K] = V[G][H]$.
:::

The resemblance between the two previous results and the theorems
@thm-lorestante and @thm-primerreciproco makes it natural to ask
what relation there is between $(\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G$
(where the quotient is taken with respect to the complete embedding
$i$) and the valuation of $\dot{\mathbb Q}$ at $G$.

::: {#lem-igualdadcomposicion}
Let $\mathbb P \in V$ be a partial order and let
$\dot{\mathbb Q} \in V$ be the $\mathbb P$-name of a partial order.
If $G$ is a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter, then
$(\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G = \{(p, \dot q) \in \mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q} : p \in G\}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the first containment. Let $(p, \dot q) \in (\mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q})/G$. Let $s \in G$ be arbitrary. Then by definition
$i(s) = (s, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$ and $(p, \dot q)$ are
compatible. Hence $s \mid p$. So by @lem-lemadenso (1) applied to
$E = \{p\} \in V$, $G \cap E \neq \emptyset$. Hence $p \in G$.

We prove the remaining containment. Let $(p, \dot q) \in \mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q}$ with $p \in G$. Let $r \in G$ be arbitrary and we
prove $i(r) = (r, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}})$ and $(p, \dot q)$
are compatible. There is $s \in G$ with $s \leq p, r$. Since
$p \Vdash \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$ and $s \leq p$, by
@lem-alguienmasfuerte (1) $s \Vdash \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$. So
$(s, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$. By @def-composicion
and @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$s \Vdash \dot q \leq \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}$. Also
$s \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q$. So
$(s, \dot q) \leq (r, \mathbb{1}_{\dot{\mathbb Q}}), (p, \dot q)$.
:::

The next result guarantees that the quotient
$(\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G$ and $\dot{\mathbb Q}_G$ always
produce the same generic extension.

::: {#thm-encajeentrecomposicion}
Let $\mathbb P, \dot{\mathbb Q}$ and $G$ be as in the previous lemma.
Then $(\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G \leq_d \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Define $e : (\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G \to \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$ by
$e(p, \dot q) = \dot q_G$ for each
$(p, \dot q) \in (\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G$.

Let $(p_1, \dot q_1), (p_2, \dot q_2) \in (\mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q})/G$ and we prove $e$ is a dense embedding.

Suppose $(p_1, \dot q_1) \leq (p_2, \dot q_2)$. Then $p_1 \leq p_2$
and $p_1 \Vdash \dot q_1 \leq \dot q_2$. Since by the previous lemma
$p_1 \in G$, $(\dot q_1)_G \leq (\dot q_2)_G$, that is,
$e(p_1, \dot q_1) \leq e(p_2, \dot q_2)$.

We prove $e$ preserves incompatibility. Suppose
$(\dot q_1)_G \mid (\dot q_2)_G$. There is
$\dot q_0 \in V^{\mathbb P}$ with $(\dot q_0)_G \in \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$
and $(\dot q_0)_G \leq (\dot q_1)_G, (\dot q_2)_G$. On one hand, by
@lem-caballito there is $(r_0, \dot q) \in \mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q}$ with $r_0 \in G$ and
$r_0 \Vdash \dot q = \dot q_0$. On the other hand, by
@thm-teoremadeforcing (2), for some $r_1 \in G$,
$r_1 \Vdash \dot q_0 \leq \dot q_1, \dot q_2$. Take $r \in G$, a
common extension of $r_0$ and $r_1$. By @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$r \Vdash \dot q = \dot q_0$ and
$r \Vdash \dot q_0 \leq \dot q_1, \dot q_2$, that is,
$r \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q_1, \dot q_2$. Since
$(p_1, \dot q_1), (p_2, \dot q_2) \in (\mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q})/G$, by @lem-igualdadcomposicion $p_1, p_2 \in G$.
By @prp-extensionparamuchos, for some $s \in G$, $s \leq p_1, p_2, r$,
so by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (2), $s \Vdash \dot q \leq \dot q_1,
\dot q_2$. Since $s \in G$, $\dot q \in \operatorname{dom}
\dot{\mathbb Q}$ and $s \Vdash \dot q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}$, by
@lem-igualdadcomposicion $(s, \dot q) \in (\mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q})/G$ and $(s, \dot q) \leq (p_1, \dot q_1),
(p_2, \dot q_2)$.

We verify $e$ is surjective, hence
$e\,{}''(\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G$ is a dense subset of
$\dot{\mathbb Q}_G$. If $q \in \dot{\mathbb Q}_G$, there is
$\dot q \in V^{\mathbb P}$ with $\dot q_G = q$. By @lem-caballito,
there is $(r, \dot q_0) \in \mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q}$ with
$r \in G$ and $r \Vdash \dot q_0 = \dot q$. By
@lem-igualdadcomposicion, $(r, \dot q_0) \in (\mathbb P *
\dot{\mathbb Q})/G$. Hence $e(r, \dot q_0) = (\dot q_0)_G = q$.
:::

It is natural to ask whether $(\mathbb P * \dot{\mathbb Q})/G$ and
$\dot{\mathbb Q}_G$ are isomorphic in general. To show the answer is
negative, we need an auxiliary notion that will simplify things.

::: {#def-predecesor-inmediato}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order. We say that $p$ is an **immediate
predecessor** of $q$ in $\mathbb P$ if and only if $p < q$ and there
is no $r \in \mathbb P$ with $p < r < q$.
:::

We now show that being an immediate predecessor is preserved under
isomorphisms.

::: {#lem-predecesores}
Let $\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ be two partial orders. If
$f : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is an isomorphism and $p$ is an
immediate predecessor of $q$ in $\mathbb P$, then $f(p)$ is an
immediate predecessor of $f(q)$ in $\mathbb Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $p$ is an immediate predecessor of $q$ in $\mathbb P$. Then
$p < q$. Since $f$ is an isomorphism, $f(p) < f(q)$.

If $f(p) < r < f(q)$ for some $r \in \mathbb Q$, we would have
$p < f^{-1}(r) < q$, that is, $p$ would not be an immediate
predecessor of $q$.
:::

Given a partial order $\mathbb P \in V$, when we refer to
$\check{\mathbb P}$ as the canonical $\mathbb P$-name of a partial
order we understand the triple $(\check{\mathbb P}, \check{\leq},
\check{\mathbb{1}}_{\mathbb P})$.

::: {#lem-ordenreducido}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order and $\check{\mathbb P}$ its
canonical $\mathbb P$-name. Then:

1. $\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P} = \{(p, \check q) : p, q \in
   \mathbb P\}$.
2. For every $(p, \check q_1), (r, \check q_2) \in \mathbb P *
   \check{\mathbb P}$, $(p, \check q_1) \leq (r, \check q_2)$ if and
   only if $p \leq r$ and $q_1 \leq q_2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1). Let $(p, \dot q) \in \mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P}$. By
@def-composicion, $p \in \mathbb P$,
$\dot q \in \operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb P}$ and
$p \Vdash \dot q \in \check{\mathbb P}$. Recall
$\check{\mathbb P} = \{(\check r, \mathbb{1}) : r \in \mathbb P\}$,
where $\mathbb{1}$ is the maximum element of $\mathbb P$. So
$\dot q \in \operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb P}$ implies
$\dot q = \check r$ for some $r \in \mathbb P$. So
$(p, \dot q) = (p, \check r)$ for some $r \in \mathbb P$.

Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$ and we show $(p, \check q) \in \mathbb P *
\check{\mathbb P}$. It remains to prove $\check q \in
\operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb P}$ and
$p \Vdash \check q \in \check{\mathbb P}$. Since $q \in \mathbb P$,
$(\check q, \mathbb{1}) \in \check{\mathbb P}$, hence
$\check q \in \operatorname{dom} \check{\mathbb P}$. Now, since
$\mathbb{1} \Vdash \check q \in \check{\mathbb P}$ and
$p \leq \mathbb{1}$, by @lem-alguienmasfuerte
$p \Vdash \check q \in \check{\mathbb P}$.

(2). By @def-composicion, $(p, \check q_1) \leq (r, \check q_2)$ if
and only if $p \leq r$ and $p \Vdash \check q_1 \leq \check q_2$.
The latter happens if and only if for every $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic
filter $G$ with $p \in G$, $(\check q_1)_G \leq (\check q_2)_G$,
equivalently, $q_1 \leq q_2$.
:::

We now show that there is a forcing notion $\mathbb P$ such that
composing it with the canonical $\mathbb P$-name of itself and
taking the quotient of this composition modulo a generic filter, the
result is a partial order not isomorphic to $\mathbb P$. This answers
our initial question negatively.

::: {#prp-pp-no-iso-p}
Let $\mathbb P := 2^{<\omega}$ and $\check{\mathbb P}$ its canonical
$\mathbb P$-name. Then $(\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G \ncong
\mathbb P$ for any $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $G$ be an arbitrary $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter. To prove
our proposition we need three preliminary observations:

(i) Let $p_0 := \{(0, 0)\}$ and $p_1 := \{(0, 1)\}$. Since
$p \leq \emptyset$ for every $p \in \mathbb P$, in particular
$p_0$ and $p_1$ are predecessors of $\emptyset$ in $\mathbb P$.

We prove $p_0$ and $p_1$ are immediate predecessors of $\emptyset$
in $\mathbb P$. If $p_k < r < \emptyset$ for some $r \in \mathbb P$
and some $k \in \{0, 1\}$, then by our order
$\emptyset \subset r \subset p_k$. The first containment gives
$0 \in \operatorname{dom} r$, while the second implies
$r(0) = p_k(0)$. Hence $r = p_k$. Observe $p_0$ and $p_1$ are
unique. If $t \in \mathbb P \setminus \{\emptyset\}$ is an
immediate predecessor of $\emptyset$, then $\operatorname{dom} t = 1$:
otherwise $\operatorname{dom} t > 1$, and then $t < p_0$ or
$t < p_1$, impossible. So $\operatorname{dom} t = 1$ and therefore
$t = p_0$ or $t = p_1$.

(ii) $p_k \in G$ for some $k < 2$.

Let $D = \{p \in \mathbb P : p \leq p_0 \text{ or } p \leq p_1\}$ and
we show this set is dense in $\mathbb P$.

Let $p \in \mathbb P$. First note $p_0 \in D$, so if $p = \emptyset$,
then $p_0 \leq p$. Suppose $p \neq \emptyset$. Then
$0 \in \operatorname{dom} p$. Since $p(0) \in \{0, 1\}$,
$p \leq p_0$ or $p \leq p_1$, hence $p \in D$ and, since $p \leq p$,
we have the desired extension in $D$.

Note $D \in V$ since both $p_0$ and $p_1$ are functions definable
in $V$. So $G \cap D \neq \emptyset$. Let $p \in G \cap D$. Then
$p \in G$ and $p \leq p_k$ for some $k < 2$. Hence $p_k \in G$.

(iii) The pairs $(\emptyset, \check p_0), (\emptyset, \check p_1)$
and $(p_k, \check{\emptyset})$ are distinct immediate predecessors
of $(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$ in $(\mathbb P *
\check{\mathbb P})/G$. By @lem-ordenreducido (1), all of these
pairs are elements of $\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P}$. Since
$\emptyset \in G$, by @lem-igualdadcomposicion these pairs are
elements of $(\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$.

By @lem-ordenreducido (2), every pair in
$(\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$ precedes
$(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$. We see that for $\ell < 2$,
$(\emptyset, \check p_\ell)$ is an immediate predecessor of
$(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$ in
$(\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$.

If some pair $(p, \check q) \in (\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$
satisfies
$(\emptyset, \check p_\ell) < (p, \check q) <
(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$, by @lem-ordenreducido (2),
$p_\ell < q < \emptyset$, contradicting (i).

We now show that $(p_k, \check{\emptyset})$ is an immediate
predecessor of $(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$. Otherwise, if some
pair $(p, \check q) \in (\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$
satisfies
$(p_k, \check{\emptyset}) < (p, \check q) <
(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$, by @lem-ordenreducido (2),
$p_k < p < \emptyset$, contradicting (i).

We prove the proposition by contradiction. Let
$f : (\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G \to \mathbb P$ be an
isomorphism.

First note $f(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset}) = \emptyset$. Since
$f^{-1}(\emptyset) \in (\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$,
$f^{-1}(\emptyset) \leq (\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$, hence
$f(f^{-1}(\emptyset)) \leq f(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$, i.e.
$\emptyset \leq f(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset})$, equivalently
$f(\emptyset, \check{\emptyset}) \subseteq \emptyset$. So the claim
holds.

Now, by (iii) and @lem-predecesores,
$f(\emptyset, \check p_0), f(\emptyset, \check p_1)$ and
$f(p_k, \check{\emptyset})$ are distinct immediate predecessors of
$\emptyset$ in $\mathbb P$, contradicting (i).
:::

By @thm-encajeentrecomposicion and the previous result, we can give
an example of two non-isomorphic partial orders each densely
embedded in the other.

::: {#prp-encaje-denso-pp}
Let $G$ be a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter. If
$\mathbb P := 2^{<\omega}$ and
$\mathbb Q := (\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P})/G$, then
$\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @prp-unnuevoreal (1) and (2), if $g = \bigcup G$, then
$g : \omega \to 2$ and $G = \{g \restriction n : n \in \omega\}$.

Note this implies $\mathbb Q = \{(g \restriction n, \check q) :
n \in \omega \,\&\, q \in \mathbb P\}$. Indeed, by
@lem-ordenreducido, $\mathbb P * \check{\mathbb P} = \{(p, \check q) :
p, q \in \mathbb P\}$. So by @lem-igualdadcomposicion,
$\mathbb Q = \{(p, \check q) : p \in G \,\&\, q \in \mathbb P\} =
\{(g \restriction n, \check q) : n \in \omega \,\&\, q \in \mathbb P\}$.

Define a function $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ by
$e(p) = (g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p, \check p)$. By the
previous observation $e(p) \in \mathbb Q$, so $e$ is well defined.
We prove $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a dense embedding.

Let $p, r \in \mathbb P$ with $p \leq r$. By @lem-ordenreducido, it
suffices to prove $g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p \leq
g \restriction \operatorname{dom} r$. By hypothesis,
$\operatorname{dom} r \leq \operatorname{dom} p$, hence
$g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p \leq g \restriction
\operatorname{dom} r$.

We prove $e\,{}''\mathbb P$ is a dense subset of $\mathbb Q$. Let
$q \in \mathbb Q$. So $q = (g \restriction n, \check p)$ for some
$n \in \omega$ and $p \in \mathbb P$. We have the following cases:

I. If $n = \operatorname{dom} p$, then $q = (g \restriction n,
\check p)$ is precisely $e(p)$ and the result holds.

II. If $n < \operatorname{dom} p$, then
$g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p \leq g \restriction n$, hence
$(g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p, \check p) \leq
(g \restriction n, \check p)$, that is, $e(p) \leq q$.

III. If $n > \operatorname{dom} p$, consider $s : n \to 2$ defined
by
$$
s(i) = \begin{cases}
p(i), & \text{if } i \in \operatorname{dom} p, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

So $s \leq p$ and $\operatorname{dom} s = n$. Hence
$(g \restriction \operatorname{dom} s, \check s) \leq
(g \restriction \operatorname{dom} p, \check p)$, i.e.
$e(s) \leq q$.
:::

## Separative quotient

The last section of this work is devoted to partial orders that
satisfy an interesting property: separativity.

::: {#def-separativo}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order. We say that $\mathbb P$ is
**separative** if and only if for every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, if
$p \nleq q$, then there is $r \in \mathbb P$ with $r \leq p$ and
$r \perp q$.
:::

The next lemma gives a comparability criterion between elements of a
separative partial order.

::: {#lem-comparabilidadseparativa}
If $\mathbb P$ is a separative partial order, then for every
$p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \leq q$ if and only if every extension of
$p$ is compatible with $q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The first implication holds since if $p \leq q$ and $r \leq p$, then
$r \leq q$, which implies $r \mid q$. The remaining implication is
verified by contrapositive: if $p \nleq q$, since $\mathbb P$ is
separative, there is $r \in \mathbb P$ with $r \leq p$ and
$r \perp q$.
:::

The connection between separativity and the relation $\Vdash$ is
established in the next result.

::: {#prp-equivalenciaseparativa}
If $\mathbb P$ is a partial order, the following are equivalent.

1. $\mathbb P$ is separative.
2. For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$: $p \Vdash \check q \in \Gamma$ if
   and only if $p \leq q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $\mathbb P$ is separative with maximum element $\mathbb{1}$.
Consider $p, q \in \mathbb P$ with $p \nleq q$. Then there is
$r \leq p$ with $r \perp q$. Now, since
$\mathbb{1} \Vdash \Gamma$ is a filter and
$r \Vdash \check r \in \Gamma$, by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1),
$r \Vdash \Gamma$ is a filter. So $r \Vdash \check q \notin \Gamma$.
Hence $p \nVdash \check q \in \Gamma$. Conversely, if $p \leq q$,
since $q \Vdash \check q \in \Gamma$, by @lem-alguienmasfuerte (1)
$p \Vdash \check q \in \Gamma$.

We prove (2) implies (1). Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$. If $p \nleq q$,
then $p \nVdash \check q \in \Gamma$. So for some $r \leq p$,
$r \Vdash \check q \notin \Gamma$. By @lem-condicionenG, we can
consider a $(V, \mathbb P)$-generic filter $G$ containing $r$.
Hence $q \notin G$. By @lem-lemadenso (1) applied to $\{q\}$,
$r_0 \perp q$ for some $r_0 \in G$. Take $r_1 \in G$, a common
extension of $r$ and $r_0$. We can claim $r_1 \perp q$: otherwise,
$s \leq r_1, q$ for some $s \in \mathbb P$, hence $s \leq r_0, q$,
impossible. So $r_1 \leq p$ and $r_1 \perp q$, that is, $\mathbb P$
is separative.
:::

The next proposition gives a sufficient condition for a complete
embedding to be injective.

::: {#prp-encaje-completo-inyectivo}
If $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$ is a complete embedding where
$\mathbb P$ and $\mathbb Q$ are two antisymmetric separative partial
orders, then:

1. $e$ is injective.
2. $e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}) = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$.
3. For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$: $p \leq q$ if and only if
   $e(p) \leq e(q)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$ with $e(p) = e(q)$. We prove $p = q$ by
contradiction. If $p \neq q$, then $p \nleq q$ or $q \nleq p$ since
$\mathbb P$ is antisymmetric. Suppose $p \nleq q$. Then there is
$r \leq p$ with $r \perp q$. Hence $e(r) \leq e(p)$ and
$e(r) \perp e(q)$. But then $e(r) \leq e(q)$ and $e(r) \perp e(q)$
since $e(p) = e(q)$, impossible. The case $q \nleq p$ is analogous.

We verify $e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}) = \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$.
Since $q \leq \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$ for every $q \in \mathbb Q$,
the inequality $e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}) \leq
\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q}$ always holds. It remains to prove
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q} \leq e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$. If not,
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q} \nleq e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$, so
$q_0 \perp e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$ for some
$q_0 \in \mathbb Q$ since $\mathbb Q$ is separative. By
@thm-equivalenciaencaje, $q_0$ admits an $e$-reduction to
$\mathbb P$, say $p$. So $e(p) \mid q_0$. Let
$s \leq e(p), q_0$. Since $p \leq \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}$,
$e(p) \leq e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$. Hence
$s \leq e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P}), q_0$, a contradiction. So
$\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb Q} \leq e(\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$.

Let $p, q \in \mathbb P$. If $p \leq q$, then $e(p) \leq e(q)$ since
$e$ is an embedding. We prove the remaining implication by
contradiction. If $e(p) \leq e(q)$ and $p \nleq q$, then $r \perp q$
for some $r \leq p$ since $\mathbb P$ is separative. So
$e(r) \leq e(p)$ and $e(r) \perp e(q)$. Since $e(p) \leq e(q)$,
$e(r) \leq e(q)$, hence $e(r) \mid e(q)$, impossible.
:::

Naturally, there are partial orders that are not separative (see the
remarks immediately following @lem-compatibilidadomega); however,
every order can be densely embedded into a separative one. The
construction of this order requires defining an equivalence relation.

::: {#def-relacionseparativa}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order and $p, q \in \mathbb P$. Then:

1. $p \sim q$ if and only if for every $r \in \mathbb P$, $r \mid p$
   if and only if $r \mid q$.
2. $[p] = \{s \in \mathbb P : s \sim p\}$.
:::

**Remark.** $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

- $\sim$ is reflexive, since $p$ is compatible with the same elements
  that are compatible with $p$.
- If $p \sim q$, since $p$ and $q$ are compatible with the same
  elements of $\mathbb P$, $q \sim p$ trivially.
- If $p \sim r$ and $r \sim q$, then $p$ and $r$ are compatible with
  the same elements of $\mathbb P$, and $r$ and $q$ are compatible
  with the same elements of $\mathbb P$. So $p$ and $q$ are
  compatible with the same elements of $\mathbb P$, that is,
  $p \sim q$.

::: {#def-ordenseparativo}
We define the **separative quotient** of a partial order $\mathbb P$
as
$$
\mathbb P/_\sim = \{[p] : p \in \mathbb P\}.
$$

Define the binary relation $\trianglelefteq$ on
$\mathbb P/_\sim$ by $[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$ if and only if for
every $r \leq p$, $r \mid q$.
:::

**Remark.** The relation $\trianglelefteq$ is well defined. Indeed,
if $[p] = [p']$, $[q] = [q']$ and $[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$, then
given $r \leq p'$, in particular $r \mid p'$. Hence $r \mid p$. Let
$p_1 \leq r, p$. Then $p_1 \mid q$ since
$[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$. Let $p_2 \leq p_1, q$. So
$p_2 \leq r, q$, i.e. $r \mid q$. Hence $r \mid q'$, so
$[p'] \trianglelefteq [q']$.

The next lemma tells us that order and incompatibility in any partial
order imply the corresponding facts in its separative quotient. For
convenience we write $\mathbb P/_\sim$ to mean
$(\mathbb P/_\sim, \trianglelefteq)$.

::: {#lem-preservacionseparativa}
If $\mathbb P$ is a partial order and $\mathbb P/_\sim$ is its
separative quotient, then for every $p, q \in \mathbb P$:

1. $p \leq q$ implies $[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$.
2. $p \perp q$ implies $[p] \perp [q]$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Suppose $p \leq q$. If $r \leq p$, then $r \leq q$, in particular
$r \mid q$. Hence $[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$, which proves (1).

We verify (2) by contrapositive. Let $[p]$ and $[q]$ be compatible.
So $[r] \trianglelefteq [p], [q]$ for some $r \in \mathbb P$. But by
@def-ordenseparativo, every extension of $r$ is compatible with $p$
and $q$. In particular, $r$ and $p$ admit a common extension, say
$s$. So $s$ and $q$ are compatible. Let $t \leq s, q$. So
$t \leq p, q$.
:::

::: {#prp-cociente-separativo-orden}
Let $\mathbb P$ be a partial order. Then $\mathbb P/_\sim$ is an
antisymmetric separative partial order.
:::

::: {.proof}
$[p] \trianglelefteq [p]$, since $r \leq p$ implies $r \mid p$ for
every $r \in \mathbb P$.

Let $p, q, r \in \mathbb P$ with $[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$ and
$[q] \trianglelefteq [r]$. Let $s \leq p$. Then $s \mid q$, so
$p_0 \leq s, q$ for some $p_0 \in \mathbb P$. So $p_0$ and $r$ are
compatible. Let $p_1 \leq p_0, r$. So $p_1 \leq s, r$. Hence
$[p] \trianglelefteq [r]$.

$\mathbb P/_\sim$ is separative: if $[p], [q] \in
\mathbb P/_\sim$ satisfy $[p] \not\trianglelefteq [q]$, by
@def-ordenseparativo there is $r \leq p$ with $r \perp q$. By
@lem-preservacionseparativa, $[r] \trianglelefteq [p]$ and
$[r] \perp [q]$.

We prove antisymmetry. Suppose $p, q \in \mathbb P$ satisfy
$[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$ and $[q] \trianglelefteq [p]$. Let
$r \in \mathbb P$ with $r \mid p$. Take $s \leq p, r$. Since
$[p] \trianglelefteq [q]$, $s \mid q$. So there is $t \leq s, q$.
Hence $t \leq r, q$. Analogously,
$[q] \trianglelefteq [p]$ implies that every condition compatible
with $q$ is compatible with $p$. So $[p] = [q]$.
:::

We use what we have done to prove that every partial order densely
embeds into its separative quotient.

::: {#thm-encaje-denso-cociente}
$\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb P/_\sim$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Define $\pi : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P/_\sim$ by $\pi(p) = [p]$.

By @lem-preservacionseparativa, $\pi$ preserves order and
incompatibility. The function $\pi : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P/_\sim$
is clearly surjective, hence $\pi\,{}''\mathbb P$ is a dense subset
of $\mathbb P/_\sim$. So $\pi$ is a dense embedding.
:::

The separative quotient has a certain uniqueness, as the next
proposition reveals.

::: {#prp-unicidadcociente}
If $(\mathbb Q, \sqsubseteq)$ is an antisymmetric separative partial
order for which there exists $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb Q$, a
surjective embedding (hence dense), then $\mathbb P/_\sim \cong
\mathbb Q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Define $f : \mathbb P/_\sim \to \mathbb Q$ by $f([p]) = e(p)$. Note
that $f$ makes commutative the diagram $\mathbb P \xrightarrow{e}
\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb P \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathbb P/_\sim
\xrightarrow{f} \mathbb Q$, since $f \circ \pi = e$.

We verify $f$ is well defined, i.e. if $p \sim r$ then
$e(p) = e(r)$. By contrapositive, if $e(p) \neq e(r)$, then
$e(p) \not\sqsubseteq e(r)$ or $e(r) \not\sqsubseteq e(p)$ since
$\mathbb Q$ is antisymmetric. Suppose the former. Since $\mathbb Q$
is separative, $q \sqsubseteq e(p)$ and $q \perp e(r)$ for some
$q \in \mathbb Q$. By surjectivity of $e$, $q = e(p_0)$ for some
$p_0 \in \mathbb P$, hence $e(p_0) \sqsubseteq e(p)$ and
$e(p_0) \perp e(r)$, that is, $p \not\sim r$. The case
$e(r) \not\sqsubseteq e(p)$ is analogous.

We prove $f$ is an isomorphism between $\mathbb P/_\sim$ and
$\mathbb Q$. $f$ is injective, since if $e(p) = e(r)$, then
$p \sim r$. Indeed, if $p \not\sim r$, then $s \mid p$ and
$s \perp r$ for some $s \in \mathbb P$. So $e(s) \mid e(p)$ and
$e(s) \perp e(r)$, hence $e(p) \neq e(r)$. So $e(p) = e(r)$ implies
$[p] = [r]$. Since $f \circ \pi = e$ and $e$ is surjective, $f$ is
too.

We prove by contrapositive in both directions that $f$ and $f^{-1}$
preserve the order. Let $[p], [r] \in \mathbb P/_\sim$ with
$[p] \trianglelefteq [r]$. Suppose $e(p) \not\sqsubseteq e(r)$.
Since $\mathbb Q$ is separative, there is $q \sqsubseteq e(p)$ with
$q \perp e(r)$. By surjectivity of $e$, $q = e(p_0)$ for some
$p_0 \in \mathbb P$, hence $e(p_0) \sqsubseteq e(p)$ and
$e(p_0) \perp e(r)$. Since $e(p_0) \sqsubseteq e(p)$ implies
$e(p_0) \mid e(p)$, $p_0 \mid p$. Let $p_1 \leq p_0, p$. So
$e(p_1) \sqsubseteq e(p_0)$. Also, $p_1$ and $r$ are incompatible:
otherwise, $p_1 \mid r$, hence $e(p_1) \mid e(r)$, i.e. there is
$q_0 \sqsubseteq e(p_1), e(r)$, hence
$q_0 \sqsubseteq e(p_0), e(r)$, impossible. So
$p_1 \in \mathbb P$ satisfies $p_1 \leq p$ and $p_1 \perp r$, that
is, $[p] \not\trianglelefteq [r]$.

Now suppose $[p] \not\trianglelefteq [r]$. By @def-ordenseparativo,
there is $p_0 \in \mathbb P$ with $p_0 \leq p$ and $p_0 \perp r$.
Hence $e(p_0) \sqsubseteq e(p)$ and $e(p_0) \perp e(r)$, i.e.
$f([p]) \not\sqsubseteq f([r])$.
:::

As a corollary of the above and @thm-igualdadextensiones, every
generic extension can be seen as the generic extension given by a
separative partial order.

Below we present an alternative way to densely embed any partial
order into a separative partial order.

::: {#def-ordenestrella}
For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$:

1. $p \leq^\star q$ if and only if for every $r \leq p$, $r \mid q$.
2. $\mathbb P^\star = (\mathbb P, \leq^\star, \mathbb{1}_{\mathbb P})$.
:::

It is interesting that clause (1) of the previous definition is
motivated by @lem-comparabilidadseparativa, so we expect
$\mathbb P^\star$ to be a separative partial order. A treatment of
separativity in terms of the relation $\leq^\star$ can be found in
[@barto]. Before proving that $\mathbb P^\star$ is separative, we
verify that order and incompatibility in $\mathbb P$ imply the
corresponding facts in $\mathbb P^\star$.

::: {#lem-implicacionestrella}
For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$:

1. $p \leq q$ implies $p \leq^\star q$.
2. $p \perp q$ implies $p \perp^\star q$ — that is, there is no
   $r \in \mathbb P^\star$ with $r \leq^\star p$ and
   $r \leq^\star q$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The first holds because given $r \leq p$, the hypothesis gives
$r \leq q$. Hence $r \mid q$.

We prove (2) by contrapositive. Suppose there is $r \in \mathbb P$
with $r \leq^\star p$ and $r \leq^\star q$. Then $r \mid p$. Let
$s \leq r, p$. So $s \mid q$ since $r \leq^\star q$. Take
$t \in \mathbb P$ with $t \leq s, q$. Hence $t \leq p, q$, as
required.
:::

::: {#prp-pestrella-separativo}
$\mathbb P^\star$ is a separative partial order.
:::

::: {.proof}
Our order is reflexive: $p \leq^\star p$ since every extension of
$p$ is compatible with $p$.

Suppose $p \leq^\star q$ and $q \leq^\star r$. We check
$p \leq^\star r$. If $s \leq p$, then $s \mid q$, so
$p_0 \leq s, q$ for some $p_0 \in \mathbb P$. So $p_0$ and $r$ are
compatible. Let $p_1 \leq p_0, r$. So $p_1 \leq s, r$, hence
$p \leq^\star r$.

Now, by @def-ordenestrella, for every $p, q \in \mathbb P$,
$p \nleq^\star q$ implies there is $r \leq p$ with $r \perp q$. By
@lem-implicacionestrella, $r \leq^\star p$ and $r \perp^\star q$.
So $\mathbb P^\star$ is separative.
:::

By the previous proposition and @prp-equivalenciaseparativa, for
every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \Vdash \check q \in \Gamma$ is
equivalent to $p \leq^\star q$.

::: {#thm-encaje-denso-pestrella}
$\mathbb P \leq_d \mathbb P^\star$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $e : \mathbb P \to \mathbb P^\star$ be the identity. By
@lem-implicacionestrella, $e$ is an embedding, and since
$e\,{}''\mathbb P = \mathbb P$, it is dense.
:::

We illustrate the constructions of this section with an example. Let
$\mathbb P = ([\omega]^\omega, \subseteq)$. We first see that two
elements in this order are compatible if and only if their
intersection is infinite.

::: {#lem-compatibilidadomega}
For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \mid q$ if and only if
$|p \cap q| = \omega$.
:::

::: {.proof}
If $p \mid q$, there is $r \in \mathbb P$ with $r \subseteq p$ and
$r \subseteq q$. So $r \subseteq p \cap q$, hence
$|p \cap q| = \omega$. Conversely, if $|p \cap q| = \omega$, then
$p \cap q \in \mathbb P$ and is a common extension of $p$ and $q$
since both contain $p \cap q$.
:::

Observe that the partial order considered is not separative. Let
$p = \omega$ and $q = \omega \setminus \{0\}$. So $p \nsubseteq q$
and yet every subset of $p$ in $\mathbb P$ is compatible with $q$.
Indeed, if $r \in \mathbb P$ and $r \subseteq p$, then
$r \cap q = r \setminus \{0\}$ since $q \subseteq p$, hence
$|r \cap q| = \omega$.

By our compatibility criterion for $\mathbb P$ and following
@def-ordenestrella, for every $p, q \in \mathbb P$:
$p \subseteq^\star q$ if and only if for every $r \in \mathbb P$,
$r \subseteq p$ implies $|r \cap q| = \omega$.

::: {#lem-subseteq-estrella}
For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \subseteq^\star q$ if and only if
$|p \setminus q| < \omega$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the first implication by contrapositive. Suppose
$p \setminus q$ is infinite. So $r := p \setminus q \in \mathbb P$,
$r \subseteq p$ and $r \perp q$, since $r \cap q = \emptyset$.

We prove the remaining implication directly. Let $r \in \mathbb P$
with $r \subseteq p$. By hypothesis, $|p \setminus q| < \omega$.
Since $r = (r \cap q) \cup (r \setminus q)$,
$|r \setminus q| < \omega$. Hence $|r \cap q| = \omega$.
:::

So $\mathbb P^\star = ([\omega]^\omega, \subseteq^\star)$. Note that
$\mathbb P^\star$ is not antisymmetric. Indeed, if $p = \omega$ and
$q = \omega \setminus \{0\}$, then $p \subseteq^\star q$ and
$q \subseteq^\star p$, since $|p \setminus q| = 1 < \omega$ and
$|q \setminus p| = 0 < \omega$. Yet $p \neq q$.

We are now interested in $\mathbb P/_\sim$, i.e. the separative
quotient of $\mathbb P$ (see @def-ordenseparativo). By
@def-relacionseparativa, two conditions $p, q \in \mathbb P$ are
related if and only if they are compatible with the same elements,
which by @lem-compatibilidadomega is equivalent to: $p \sim q$ if
and only if for every $r \in \mathbb P$,
$|p \cap r| = |q \cap r| = \omega$. The latter lets us state:

::: {#prp-simetrica-diferencia}
For every $p, q \in \mathbb P$, $p \sim q$ if and only if
$|p \bigtriangleup q| < \omega$, where $p \bigtriangleup q =
(p \setminus q) \cup (q \setminus p)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We prove the first implication by contrapositive. If
$|p \bigtriangleup q| = \omega$, then $|p \setminus q| = \omega$ or
$|q \setminus p| = \omega$. If $|p \setminus q| = \omega$, then
$p \setminus q$ is an element of $\mathbb P$ for which
$|p \cap (p \setminus q)| = \omega$ and
$|q \cap (p \setminus q)| = 0 < \omega$, hence $p \not\sim q$. The
case $|q \setminus p| = \omega$ is analogous.

Suppose $|p \bigtriangleup q| < \omega$. Let $r \in \mathbb P$ be
compatible with $q$, i.e. $|r \cap q| = \omega$. Since
$r \cap q = (r \cap q \cap p) \cup (r \cap q \setminus p)$ and by
hypothesis $|q \setminus p| < \omega$,
$|r \cap q \cap p| = \omega$. Since $r \cap q \cap p \subseteq
r \cap p$, $|r \cap p| = \omega$. An analogous argument shows every
element compatible with $p$ is also compatible with $q$.
:::

In other contexts the quotient $\mathbb P/_\sim$ presented here is
denoted $([\omega]^\omega, \subseteq)/\mathrm{fin}$, for which there
is an extensive literature. By @prp-cociente-separativo-orden,
$\mathbb P/_\sim$ is an antisymmetric partial order. So
$\mathbb P/_\sim$ and $\mathbb P^\star$ cannot be isomorphic. This
shows that antisymmetry cannot be dropped from
@prp-unicidadcociente.
